tagline.text: Site of the Cry that tore the cedula, newly renovated in 2026

location.label: Location
location.text: Seminary Road, Bahay Toro (Project 8), Quezon City

children.text: This commemorative park in Quezon City honors the Cry of Pugad Lawin, when Andrés Bonifacio and the Katipuneros are recorded as tearing their cedulas in defiance of Spain in August 1896. Sculptures of the Katipuneros by National Artist Napoleon Abueva stand here, and the shrine reopened after a renovation timed to the 130th anniversary in August 2026.

Pugad Lawin Shrine is a historical commemorative park on Seminary Road in Barangay Bahay Toro, Project 8, Quezon City. In Filipino, "Pugad Lawin" means hawk's nest, and the site is commemorated as the place of the Cry of Pugad Lawin (Sigaw ng Pugad Lawin), which marked the start of the Philippine Revolution against Spanish colonial rule. According to the Quezon City government, on
August 23, 1896

Andrés Bonifacio and members of the Katipunan (a secret revolutionary society opposed to Spanish rule) tore up their cedulas, the identity documents of the colonial era, in protest. The shrine was developed in 1998 on the site of the house of Juan Ramos, son of Melchora Aquino (Tandang Sora). The name may be unfamiliar to many foreign travelers, but this scene is frequently cited in Philippine revolutionary history, and the shrine is regarded as a place for learning about it. If you think of it as the starting point of a protest against colonial rule, much like Korea's March 1st Movement, it is easier to relate to.
That said, historians still debate exactly when and where the Cry took place. According to Wikipedia, from 1908 to 1963 it was believed to have happened in Balintawak on
August 26
, and in 1963 the government fixed
August 23

and the present location in Quezon City. Pío Valenzuela, who testified that he was present, said it was held at Pugad Lawin, the land of Juan Ramos, and a research team found that spot in 1940, but opinions differ on whether it is the same as today's site. It is therefore most accurate to think of this place not as the single confirmed location but as the one the government officially recognizes and commemorates. In 1984 the National Historical Institute (NHI) set up a marker on Seminary Road behind Toro Hills High School.
What changed the site noticeably came in 2026. On
August 23, 2026

, the 130th anniversary of the Cry, the Quezon City government unveiled the renovated shrine, and local media reported that Mayor Joy Belmonte, officials of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP), and descendants of Emilio Jacinto and Melchora Aquino attended. The design is by the architecture studio Arc Lico. It starts from the moment a cedula is torn, with split curves that open outward, and the studio describes it as "rupture becomes passage." The center is a circle that stands for an early form of public gathering and also draws on the curve of the Baybayin letter "K."

The park holds statues of the Katipuneros (Katipunan members) made by National Artist Napoleon Abueva. In the renovation, the Castrillo foundry restored these sculptures and set them on a low civic platform. Local media report about 27 bronze statues that include men, women and children. Curved walls, ramps, paths and exhibition areas are gathered here so that you walk from gathering to commemoration and then to historical reflection, and there are also ramps that wheelchairs and strollers can use. As the description of low structures tucked beneath mature trees suggests, there is plenty of shade, and the place feels calm even in the middle of the city. It is not a large attraction. About an hour is enough even at a relaxed pace, and many visitors pair it with the Tandang Sora National Shrine and Women's Museum in the same area and Quezon Memorial Circle for a half-day history route. It suits anyone curious about modern Philippine history or the background of National Heroes Day, the public holiday in late August. Opening hours and admission may have changed after the renovation, so check with the Quezon City tourism office before you go. For photos, framing the statues against the curved wall in front of them fits both the sculpture and the new design in one shot. Signs may mix Filipino and English, so a translation app can help.

Bronze sculptures by National Artist Napoleon Abueva are the centerpiece. They are described as showing men, women and children who joined the revolution, and the Castrillo foundry restored them in the 2026 renovation. Step close and look at the faces and the folds of the clothing.

blocks.title: A new design based on the moment a cedula is torn

children.text: The Arc Lico studio shaped the space with curves that split and open outward. The circular plaza at the center evokes early public gatherings, and the curve recalls the Baybayin "K." Knowing the design idea makes the flow of the paths look different as you walk.

The new shrine is described as an interpretation space where visitors ask questions and learn, not a reconstruction of the past. The curved walls and exhibition areas follow the order you walk in, so move slowly and read the panels one by one.

A marker set up by the National Historical Institute in 1984 shows that this area is an officially commemorated site. Standing in front of it and recalling the debate over the exact place makes the story richer.

blocks.title: The setting of Juan Ramos's house

children.text: The shrine is described as built in 1998 on the site of the house of Juan Ramos, son of Tandang Sora. Seen together with the nearby Tandang Sora National Shrine, it continues the story of the same family and the revolution.

blocks.title: A shaded walk in the city

children.text: Ramps and paths built low beneath mature trees make it relatively comfortable to walk even on hot days. The shrine is described as having ramps for strollers and wheelchairs.

The Cry of the revolution is commemorated on National Heroes Day, a public holiday on the last Monday of August. Commemorative events are sometimes held in late August, so if your schedule allows it is a good way to feel the local atmosphere.

items.title: Half-day history route
items.subtitle: From Pugad Lawin to Tandang Sora

children.text: Arrive at Pugad Lawin Shrine when it opens. You avoid the midday heat, and you can confirm the latest opening hours at the information desk.
See the marker first, then walk once around the central plaza and the Katipunero statues. Move slowly through the curved walls and exhibition areas, reading the panels.
Take a taxi or ride-hailing car to the Tandang Sora National Shrine. It is about
3.6 km
in a straight line, and travel time varies a lot with traffic.
Visit the bronze statue and the Women's Museum at the Tandang Sora National Shrine. Check the museum's opening hours and fees on site.
Have lunch nearby, then finish with a walk at Quezon Memorial Circle.
Travel can take a long time, so plan around rush hours.

items.title: Relaxed route
items.subtitle: A full day of Quezon City history

children.text: Visit Pugad Lawin Shrine and get the story of the revolution's start straight.
Visit the Tandang Sora National Shrine and Women's Museum.
Look around the Quezon Memorial Shrine and park at Quezon Memorial Circle.
Head back to your hotel while avoiding the rush-hour jam.
The simplest way from central Manila (Ermita, Malate, Makati) is a taxi or ride-hailing car to Seminary Road, Bahay Toro, Project 8, near Toro Hills High School.
By public transport, go to a railway station on the northern trunk line in Quezon City, then transfer to a jeepney or tricycle. Routes and fares can change, so confirm locally.
Traffic between central Manila and Quezon City is heavy at times, so travel time varies a lot.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), take a taxi or ride-hailing car to Quezon City. Travel time varies a lot with traffic.
Around the shrine you can get about by tricycle and jeepney. In your ride-hailing app, search for "Pugad Lawin Shrine" and set it as the destination.
The dry season from December to May is best for walking. The park is mostly outdoors, so rainy days can be inconvenient.
Commemorative events for the Cry are often held in late August. On event days, however, it gets crowded and some areas may be closed off.

The shrine itself has no lodging or restaurants, and the surroundings are residential. The easiest approach is to base yourself in central Manila or central Quezon City and visit as a day trip. Quezon City has good public transport links, so choosing a hotel close to a metro or light rail station makes getting around easier.
You can eat at neighborhood restaurants nearby or around Quezon Memorial Circle. Bring water and snacks before traveling in the midday heat.

This is not a place where you stay for long, so it works best to combine it with other Quezon City sights and plan your meals before or after. Local restaurants may change their hours, so check on a map app before heading out.
According to the Quezon City government, hours are listed as Tuesday to Sunday, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., but they may have changed after the 2026 renovation, so check before you go.
It may be closed on Mondays, so it is safest to avoid visiting on a Monday.
Groups of more than 10 need to book in advance. The Quezon City tourism office number is 8988-4242.
For a taxi or ride-hailing destination, enter "Pugad Lawin Shrine, Seminary Road, Bahay Toro."
Knowing that the place and date of the Cry are debated makes the explanations much more interesting to read.
There is plenty of shade, but it is hot at midday. Bring a hat and water.
Pairing it with the Tandang Sora National Shrine and Quezon Memorial Circle makes for a good route.
Opening hours and admission may have changed after the August 2026 renovation, so check the latest notice.
The road from Manila to Quezon City is very congested at rush hour. Leave yourself extra time.
The park is in a residential area and can be quiet late in the evening. Leave before dark.
Showers and typhoons in the rainy season can cancel outdoor plans.
Keep your belongings close, and check the plate number in the app before getting into a ride-hailing car.
Some areas may be closed off on event days.

blocks.title: Tandang Sora National Shrine and Women's Museum

children.text: A shrine and museum honoring Melchora Aquino, the Mother of the Revolution, about
3.6 km
away in a straight line. You can follow the same revolutionary story from Pugad Lawin.
An urban retreat with the Quezon Memorial Shrine and a park, about
3.7 km
away in a straight line. A good place to walk, eat and rest.
A forest and reservoir park in northern Quezon City. Good if you want to follow the history route with some nature.

blocks.title: Monument at Vinzons Hall, UP Diliman

children.text: According to Wikipedia, an old monument from Balintawak was dismantled in 1968 and re-erected the same November in front of Vinzons Hall on the UP Diliman campus. It lets you follow the debate over where the Cry happened.
